bigPicture: The White House said Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin plan an unprecedented three-way meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday to discuss nuclear arms and the Iran war, while Poland joined Britain, France, Germany and Italy in Europe's team for the next Ukraine talks. Wall Street ended a strong week on a weak note as tech shares and Bitcoin fell and the 10-year US yield held near 5.15% on bets of a December Fed rate rise. In the US, a communications failure grounded all departing flights for nearly five hours, and the country lost its measles-free status after 26 years. Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed two tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz, without independent confirmation. Beyond the headlines, Congo's Ebola response is being held back by armed attacks, a baby died of cold in Gaza's tent camps, and Nigeria's diphtheria epidemic reached a boarding school. Russian strikes on Ukraine's power grid left almost 50,000 households in the Odesa region without electricity.

stories.everyday: No immediate change in daily life, but talks between these three leaders can move oil prices (through the Iran war), the dollar and defence spending. For Poland, any hint that Ukraine's future is discussed over Kyiv's head matters for security on the eastern border.
stories.rankWhy: A first-ever meeting of the leaders of the three biggest nuclear powers could shape arms control, the Iran war and the Ukraine diplomacy that affect billions of people and global markets.
stories.title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented three-way meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday, with nuclear arms and Iran on the agenda
stories.what: The White House said on Friday that US President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin plan to meet on Thursday 19 November on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. AP described it as the first gathering of the heads of the world's three biggest nuclear powers. A senior US official said Trump wants to discuss the US war with Iran and a three-way deal on nuclear arsenals, called the meeting the 'beginning of hopefully a conversation' on disarmament and said no agreement is expected. Ukraine is not expected to be on the agenda, the official said, describing it as 'a whole other track'. Before Shenzhen, Trump leaves on Monday for Manila for a Quad meeting and a US–ASEAN summit, and meets Xi on Thursday, according to Anadolu.
stories.why: The New START treaty, the last cap on US and Russian nuclear warheads, expired in February, AP noted; Trump rejected a Russian offer of a one-year extension and wants a new deal that includes China. AP put China's arsenal at more than 600 warheads against over 5,000 each for the US and Russia, which is why Beijing has shown little interest in joining limits. Analysts quoted by AP expect symbolism rather than breakthroughs: Xi can showcase China's clout and the Kremlin can present Russia as a peer of Washington and Beijing. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy worries his country could be discussed without Kyiv, AP reported.

All three still gained over the week: roughly 2.5% for the S&P 500, 2.3% for the Nasdaq and 2.1% for the Dow. Technology was the weakest sector (−1.7%) while consumer staples (+1.4%) and energy (+1.0%) led. Nvidia closed about 2% lower and its stock-market value fell back below $4 trillion, down roughly 12% on the week after CEO Jensen Huang's resignation; AMD closed about 8.75% lower. The 10-year Treasury yield (the interest rate the US government pays to borrow for 10 years) closed at about 5.15%, and Bitcoin fell below $70,000 for the first time in nearly three months.
stories.why: Investors expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December: CME FedWatch data cited by Investing.com showed markets no longer pricing a hold after hotter-than-expected October consumer prices, and Friday's producer-price data put annual wholesale inflation at 6.5%. Higher yields make future company profits worth less today, which hits richly valued tech shares hardest. Yahoo Finance reported that HSBC downgraded Nvidia to Hold and cut its price target to $170 from $365, saying investor confidence had been 'shaken'. A Bitget analyst quoted by Yahoo Finance linked Bitcoin's fall to risk aversion, outflows from spot Bitcoin funds and the unwinding of leveraged bets.

stories.title: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say two 'violating' tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz; there is no independent confirmation
stories.what: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy said in a statement posted on Friday night, local time, that two oil tankers, one of them a supertanker, exploded and caught fire after hitting naval mines while using an 'unauthorised' route through the Strait of Hormuz with their tracking systems switched off, AFP and IANS reported. It warned shipowners that vessels not coordinating with Iran's traffic-control centre would meet the same fate. The ships were not named, and there was no independent confirmation, no casualty report and no comment from the shipowners. Iran's army made a similar claim on Thursday, and the US says it has cleared mines from much of the strait. This came a day after US Central Command said it shot down two Iranian drones heading for Bahrain and denied Iran's claim to have destroyed a US radar there.
stories.why: Since the US–Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February, Iran has tried to control which ships pass through the strait, and the US has blockaded Iranian ports, according to AFP. Claims like this are a way of deterring tanker traffic even without proof, which keeps a risk premium in oil prices. At the same time, Gulf News reported that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said further military action against Iran was unnecessary because economic pressure was weakening Tehran, while Iran told the UN that any renewed attack would bring retaliation.

stories.everyday: Travellers from Europe, including Poland, to the US faced knock-on delays, and Latin American airlines such as Avianca and Copa warned customers. Airline shares fell late in Friday's session.
stories.rankWhy: A nationwide halt of US departures disrupted travel for hundreds of thousands of passengers and exposed weaknesses in critical infrastructure in the world's biggest aviation market.
stories.title: US halts all departing flights for more than four hours after a communications failure at air-traffic control centres; more than 10,000 flights delayed
stories.what: The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop shortly before 4 p.m. New York time on Friday (about 22:00 in Warsaw) after what Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called a 'communication issue' affecting all of the country's Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which guide planes between airports. Departures were held while about 3,000 planes already in the air were allowed to land. The stop was lifted after more than four hours, The Rio Times reported (TVN24 put it at nearly five). By 5:45 p.m. New York time more than 10,300 flights had been delayed and more than 1,300 cancelled, Fox Weather reported. It was the first nationwide US ground stop since January 2023.
stories.why: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of an attack and that a telecommunications outage was to blame. Duffy blamed old technology and overloaded routers, and the FBI was checking whether a software update caused the outage, The Rio Times reported. Al Jazeera noted that the US air-traffic control system has suffered repeated equipment failures and staff shortages; Congress approved $12.5 billion for an overhaul last year, and on Friday the FAA and White House asked for another $30.1 billion.

stories.everyday: Measles can travel with any passenger. In Poland, too, doctors have warned that refusals of childhood vaccines weaken herd immunity; checking that children have both MMR doses is the main protection.
stories.rankWhy: Losing measles elimination status after 26 years signals that a dangerous, vaccine-preventable disease is spreading continuously in a country of 340 million people, with risks for neighbours and travellers.
stories.title: The US loses its measles-free status after 26 years as cases pass 5,000 this year
stories.what: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization's office for the Americas, has revoked the United States' measles elimination status, The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter; PAHO did not immediately respond to Reuters. 'Elimination' means no continuous local spread of the same virus strain for at least 12 months. The US had held the status since 2000. As of Thursday the CDC counted 5,182 confirmed cases in 2026 across 45 states, New York City and Washington DC, Reuters reported (Anadolu cited about 5,400), already more than double 2025's 2,289. About 7,500 people have been infected and 13 have died since 2025, according to Reuters.
stories.why: Measles is so contagious that about 95% of people need to be vaccinated to stop outbreaks; two doses of the vaccine protect about 97% of people, Reuters noted. Noel Brewer, who chairs the independent committee that presented the US findings to PAHO, said the outbreaks were 'all due to low measles vaccination coverage'. Reuters linked the surge to falling immunisation rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has questioned the vaccine's safety without scientific evidence.

stories.everyday: For Poland, a place at the table means a direct voice on ceasefire terms and security guarantees next door. A larger EU financing role for Ukraine could also mean bigger contributions from national budgets.
stories.rankWhy: Europe gaining a seat in US–Russia–Ukraine talks, with Poland in the team, could shape the terms of any ceasefire on the EU's eastern border.
stories.title: Poland joins Britain, France, Germany and Italy in the European team for the next Ukraine talks; the Kremlin has not confirmed it will accept them
stories.what: EU leaders meeting in Dublin agreed that Europe will be represented at the next round of US–Ukraine–Russia talks by the 'E5' (Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland) together with the EU institutions, European Council President António Costa announced on Friday. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Poland would play a key role in this format, TVN24 reported. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who met Vladimir Putin in Moscow on 12 November, said Putin had agreed to European participation, and a European delegation is expected at the next round in Abu Dhabi next week, RTÉ reported. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said a decision would depend on Europe showing genuine readiness to contribute. Leaders also said the EU will soon propose a 22nd package of sanctions on Russia.
stories.why: Russian, Ukrainian and US officials met in Abu Dhabi this week for the first time in nine months, but Russia excluded Europeans from the negotiations, RTÉ reported. Europe wants a say because any settlement affects its own security and its money: Ukraine faces an estimated €70 billion financing gap in 2027, which the European Commission is due to propose how to close, and leaders will discuss it on 26–27 November. Costa said only Ukraine has the legitimacy to decide on its territory.

stories.everyday: Power cuts in Ukraine affect families, hospitals and businesses through the winter, and can add to pressure on people to leave; Poland hosts many Ukrainian refugees.
stories.rankWhy: Repeated Russian strikes on Ukraine's power grid leave hundreds of thousands facing blackouts as winter begins.
stories.title: Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy grid leave almost 50,000 households in the Odesa region without power; outages spread to Sumy and Kyiv region
stories.what: A Russian attack hit a DTEK energy facility in the north of the Odesa region on 14 November, leaving almost 50,000 households without electricity, the region's military administration head Oleg Kiper confirmed, UNN reported. Emergency outages also hit part of the Sumy region and the Bucha, Fastiv and Obukhiv districts near Kyiv, while Kyiv city was under scheduled 'stabilisation' outages ordered by the grid operator.
stories.why: Russia has repeatedly targeted power substations and generation this autumn, Kyiv Post and Euromaidan Press reported, and damaged equipment takes time to repair, so grid operators ration power through scheduled outages. The attacks continue even as US envoys push for new talks, showing that diplomacy has not yet reduced the fighting.

stories.everyday: If the pipeline were seriously damaged, more Saudi oil would be stuck, which would push up fuel prices worldwide, including in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: Attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline target the main export route that bypasses Hormuz, so even unconfirmed strikes matter for oil supply.
stories.title: Yemen's Houthis claim new drone strikes on Riyadh's airport and a pumping station on Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline
stories.what: On Friday Houthi spokesman Yahya Sarea said one drone targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and two drones hit Pumping Station No. 3 on the East-West pipeline, east of Riyadh, according to House of Saud, a Saudi-focused news site. Saudi authorities and Aramco had not commented by Saturday morning and no damage was confirmed. Earlier in the week the Houthis claimed attacks on Pumping Station No. 7 and the Yanbu oil terminal; the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted several missiles and drones, and on Monday Saudi Arabia said an attack on the pipeline caused a fire without affecting operations, The New Arab reported.
stories.why: With the Strait of Hormuz restricted, the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu has become Saudi Arabia's main alternative export route, carrying about 4 million barrels a day of its roughly 7 million capacity, House of Saud reported. The Houthis, an Iran-aligned group, have regularly targeted Saudi Arabia since fighting resumed in July, The New Arab said, so hitting the pipeline is a way to raise pressure on the world's biggest oil exporter.

stories.everyday: Many Polish offices, schools and public bodies use Microsoft 365, so an outage can stop email and online meetings; keeping a backup way to contact colleagues helps.
stories.rankWhy: The outage showed how much governments, hospitals and firms in dozens of countries depend on one cloud provider.
stories.title: Microsoft blames a network capacity upgrade for its global outage; Japan's government lost email and New Zealand paused visa processing
stories.what: Microsoft apologised for the outage of Outlook, Teams and Copilot that began late on Thursday, saying it stemmed from a network capacity upgrade and was not caused by a cyberattack or AI, Anadolu reported; services were recovering by Friday. Downdetector recorded disruption in 74 countries and territories, Anadolu said. In Japan, government email went down and officials switched to phone calls and chats, Digital Minister Toshiharu Furukawa said, while New Zealand's immigration service suspended all visa processing. Australian police, the ASIO intelligence agency and some courts were also affected.
stories.why: Earlier, Microsoft said elevated loads on its infrastructure caused connectivity problems and that servers brought back online could fail again once traffic returned, so it throttled traffic while restoring capacity, TheJournal.ie and Anadolu reported. Because millions of organisations run on the same cloud services, a fault in one company's network becomes a problem for whole governments, a risk known as concentration risk.

stories.everyday: The risk to Europe is very low, but outbreaks that run for months raise the chance of spread to neighbouring countries and strain global health funding.
stories.rankWhy: Congo's largest-ever Ebola outbreak, with more than 11,000 cases, is being prolonged by armed attacks that endanger health workers and millions of people.
stories.title: UN says armed groups are now killing more people than Ebola in parts of eastern Congo, holding back the response to the country's largest outbreak
stories.what: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, declared in May and caused by the Bundibugyo virus, has passed 11,000 confirmed cases and 5,000 deaths, with about 400–500 new infections a week, UN News reported on Friday. Transmission has fallen sharply in former hotspots in Ituri province, but cases are appearing in remote rural areas. UN Ebola coordinator Julien Harneis said fighters of the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) had recently killed more people than Ebola; one attack in Cantine-Aloya, North Kivu, killed 66 civilians including three health workers.
stories.why: Stopping Ebola depends on contact tracing (finding and checking everyone an infected person met), which is very dangerous where armed groups operate, the UN said. Attacks on treatment centres and burial teams also make communities fearful, and WHO chief Tedros said some people see Ebola as a smaller threat than the violence they face. The World Food Programme said nearly 29 million people in Congo face acute food insecurity, which weakens resistance to disease.

stories.everyday: Humanitarian appeals for Gaza, including by Polish charities, focus on tents, blankets and heating fuel this winter.
stories.rankWhy: About 1.4 million people living in tents face winter floods and cold, with rising infections, while aid deliveries remain restricted.
stories.title: A nine-month-old baby dies of hypothermia in Gaza, the first cold-related death of the winter, as the WHO warns of rising infections
stories.what: Gaza's Health Ministry said on Friday that nine-month-old Kinan Ahmed Arqiq died of severe hypothermia, the first recorded cold-related death this winter, The National and Anadolu reported. About 1.4 million people, 65% of the population, live in tents or temporary shelters, according to UN OCHA figures cited by The National, and the WHO said nearly one million displaced people live in flood-exposed areas. WHO representative Reinhilde Van De Weerdt said acute respiratory infections were 33,000 cases higher than a year earlier. UN aid chief Tom Fletcher said 150,000 tents were stuck in warehouses at Gaza's borders, Democracy Now! reported.
stories.why: Dozens of countries led by Britain, Qatar and Jordan have urged Israel to lift restrictions on shelter items, fuel and other supplies; the British ambassador said these restrictions prevent aid groups from working at the needed scale. Israel's aid agency COGAT said it had stepped up sanitation work with international organisations before the rains, The National reported. Cold, crowding and flooded camps spread respiratory and water-borne disease, which is why the WHO expects infections to rise further.

stories.everyday: Poland is an ICC member and helps fund it; the court's ability to investigate powerful countries shapes how much weight its rulings carry, including in cases about the war in Ukraine.
stories.rankWhy: The ruling ends the only international court inquiry that could have examined alleged crimes by US forces in Afghanistan, a landmark for international justice and US–ICC relations.
stories.title: ICC judges close the part of the Afghanistan investigation that could have covered US troops; the prosecutor's office has appealed
stories.what: Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague ordered the closure of the original Afghanistan investigation, which included alleged crimes by US troops and intelligence operatives as well as by the Islamic State's Khorasan branch, Al Jazeera and Anadolu reported; the decision was made on Thursday and published on Friday. A separate probe into crimes by the Taliban since August 2021 continues; the court issued four arrest warrants for Taliban leaders last year. The prosecutor's office said it has already appealed.
stories.why: The judges cited 'significant limitations' on the prosecution's ability to investigate and gather evidence, Al Jazeera reported. The US is not an ICC member, does not recognise its jurisdiction and has sanctioned 13 current and former court staff; US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Trump will never allow the court to prosecute Americans. Investigating citizens of a non-member state whose government refuses to cooperate is very hard in practice.

stories.everyday: Southeast Asia is a growing source of goods sold in Poland, from electronics to clothing, so its energy costs and stability affect supply chains and prices.
stories.rankWhy: Leaders of ASEAN's 11 Southeast Asian members meet with the US, China and others as high oil prices squeeze their economies.
stories.title: ASEAN meets in Manila under pressure from the Middle East energy shock, Myanmar's war and South China Sea tensions
stories.what: The Philippines hosts the 49th ASEAN summit and related meetings, with foreign ministers meeting from Saturday and the leaders' summit running from 15 November to the 17th (Jakarta Post) or 18th (Philstar); sources differ on the final day. On 16–17 November ASEAN leaders meet counterparts from Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia and the United States, and the Philippines hands the chair to Singapore on 17 November. Topics include the economic fallout of the Middle East conflict, Myanmar's civil war and a long-delayed code of conduct for the South China Sea, which negotiators describe as about 70% complete.
stories.why: Southeast Asian countries import much of their fuel, so higher oil prices since the Iran war have raised costs for households and firms and added to inflation, the Jakarta Post reported; a shared oil stockpile is under study. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said ASEAN 'needs to act as one'. The Myanmar conflict has killed about 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million, according to UN estimates cited by the paper.

stories.everyday: The same lesson as with measles in the US: when vaccination coverage falls, old diseases return. Poland's childhood vaccine schedule includes diphtheria.
stories.rankWhy: Nigeria's diphtheria epidemic has passed 28,000 cases and 1,100 deaths, mostly among children, and now hits a boarding school of over 2,000 pupils.
stories.title: Diphtheria reaches a Kano boarding school as Nigeria's outbreak passes 28,000 cases and 1,126 deaths
stories.what: The Kano State Centre for Disease Control confirmed 12 diphtheria cases at First Lady College, Mariri, a boarding school with more than 2,000 students, after testing 313 suspected cases, The Gazette Nigeria reported on Friday. Nationally the outbreak had reached 28,151 cases and 1,126 deaths as of 7 November, according to Nigeria's NCDC figures cited by the IFRC and Anadolu, across 26 states and the capital territory; Kano alone has about 43% of cases. About two-thirds of confirmed patients were unvaccinated.
stories.why: Diphtheria is a bacterial infection that can block the airway; it is preventable with routine childhood vaccines, so outbreaks follow gaps in vaccination, health authorities said. Kano's disease-control chief Muhammad Abbas said the school needs mass vaccination but vaccine supplies are inadequate. Crowded boarding schools let the bacteria spread quickly between children aged 5–14, the group most affected.

stories.everyday: Sudan's war is one of the world's biggest displacement crises, and its refugees affect aid budgets and migration routes towards Europe.
stories.rankWhy: Control of road links between Kordofan and Darfur shapes the course of a war that has displaced millions of Sudanese.
stories.title: Sudan's army and allied forces say they recaptured the town of Al-Khuway in West Kordofan, a route towards RSF-held Darfur
stories.what: Sudan's army and the Joint Force, an alliance of former Darfur rebel groups fighting alongside it, said on Friday they had recaptured Al-Khuway in West Kordofan, as well as nearby Sarif Ankoush and other villages, from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Radio Tamazuj reported. A Joint Force spokesman claimed the RSF lost a commander and dozens of combat vehicles; these claims could not be independently verified and the RSF could not be reached. The RSF had taken the town in May 2025.
stories.why: Al-Khuway lies on roads linking North and West Kordofan with Darfur, so holding it helps move troops and supplies and could support army advances into RSF-held Darfur, Radio Tamazuj reported. The war between the army and the RSF began in April 2023 and has killed tens of thousands and displaced millions, according to humanitarian agencies.

stories.everyday: A firmer dollar makes dollar-priced goods such as fuel and electronics more expensive in złoty; the NBP dollar rate was close to 4 zł on Friday.
stories.rankWhy: A stronger dollar and weaker gold reflect the global repricing towards higher US interest rates, which affects currencies and savers worldwide.
stories.title: The dollar posts its best week since early October while gold falls about 4.6% in a week as markets price a Fed hike
stories.what: The US dollar index, which measures the dollar against six major currencies, ended the week at about 103.41, up 0.7% and its best week since early October, Stocktwits reported. US two-year Treasury yields rose about 35 basis points (0.35 percentage points) over the week to 4.86%. Spot gold steadied on Friday at about $3,883 an ounce, but was down about 4.6% over seven days and about 14% over six months, according to market data cited by Eurasia Business News.
stories.why: Fed officials including Governor Christopher Waller turned more hawkish (favouring higher rates) after a third straight month of hotter-than-expected consumer prices, and markets fully priced a December rate rise, Stocktwits reported. Higher US rates attract money into dollar assets; gold pays no interest, so it becomes relatively less attractive when yields rise, as The Rio Times noted.

stories.everyday: River and sea cruises are popular with older travellers, including Poles; the investigation may lead to new rules for ships passing docked vessels.
stories.rankWhy: A collision on the Mississippi River hurt dozens of passengers and raised questions about safety on one of the world's busiest inland waterways.
stories.title: A tanker that lost steering hits a docked river cruise ship in New Orleans; 32 passengers hospitalised and all aboard accounted for
stories.what: The tanker Atlantic Asphalt struck American Cruise Lines' river cruiser American Heritage, docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans, at about 12:30 p.m. local time on Friday, according to the Port of New Orleans cited by Fox News. The cruiser took on water and capsized as people evacuated; 32 passengers were taken to hospital, none in critical condition, and officials said everyone aboard was accounted for. Port officials first reported about 129 passengers plus crew; Mayor Helena Moreno later estimated 180–190 people were aboard.
stories.why: Officials said the tanker lost control; Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham said investigators were looking at an apparent loss of steering, but the cause is not yet known. The National Transportation Safety Board sent a team, expected on Saturday morning.

stories.everyday: Anyone's voice can be copied from recordings online; the ruling suggests Polish courts treat a voice as part of a person's protected identity.
stories.rankWhy: A first-instance ruling that an AI-cloned voice violates personal rights could become a reference point for how Polish law treats deepfakes.
stories.title: Warsaw court rules that an advert with an AI-cloned voice of a well-known lektor violated his personal rights
stories.what: The Warsaw District Court ordered the company JFC Polska to remove online advertisements for home sewage treatment plants that used an AI-generated voice resembling that of voice-over artist (lektor) Jarosław Łukomski, to publish an apology and to pay him about 47,280 zł in compensation and damages, Rzeczpospolita and TVN24 reported. Łukomski said he never recorded the ad, consented or was paid. The ruling is not final; the company, which denies deliberately violating his rights, had not said whether it will appeal.
stories.why: The court based its decision on the protection of personal rights (dobra osobiste) in Polish civil law, focusing on content a listener could take as genuine, Rzeczpospolita reported. Cheap voice-cloning tools make such cases easier to create, and Łukomski said he hopes the case leads to changes in Polish law.

stories.everyday: Political stability in Nigeria, a major oil producer and Africa's most populous nation, affects migration, energy markets and investment.
stories.rankWhy: Rising political violence before Nigeria's 2027 elections matters for Africa's most populous country, though this incident is disputed.
stories.title: Videos appear to show stones thrown at President Tinubu's convoy in Abuja; his aide calls them misleading
stories.what: Footage shared by opposition politician Dino Melaye appeared to show young men throwing stones at a convoy said to be President Bola Tinubu's after Friday prayers at a mosque in Abuja, with voices chanting a Hausa phrase meaning 'we don't want you', Legit.ng reported. Presidential aide O'tega Ogra called the videos misleading, blamed opposition actors and released a video showing supporters greeting Tinubu. In a statement on Friday, Tinubu ordered security agencies to crack down on political thuggery and violence ahead of the 2027 elections, Naija News reported.
stories.why: Nigeria votes in early 2027 (the electoral commission has set governorship polls for 6 February 2027, according to a court case reported by Naija News), and campaigning has been marked by clashes between rival supporters. Neither side's footage has been independently verified.

stories.everyday: Travellers to Paris should expect closed metro stations and road disruption on Saturday.
stories.rankWhy: Tens of thousands are expected to march in Paris over living costs, policing and children's rights, six months before France's presidential election.
stories.title: Paris braces for marches on cost of living, a police weapons bill and children's rights; another march calls for an AI treaty
stories.what: Several groups plan to march in Paris on Saturday 14 November, Sortiraparis reported: a 'Yellow Vests' coordination protesting the rising cost of living, a children's-rights movement, and opponents of a bill that would presume police officers use their weapons lawfully, joined by unions including the CGT, FSU and FO, on a route from Place de la République to Place de la Nation. A separate march organised by Pause IA and Stop The AI Race calls for an international treaty on artificial intelligence. A police intelligence memo expected 30,000–60,000 people, and 21 metro stations were to be closed.
stories.why: The children's-rights movement explicitly links its march to the presidential election six months away, Sortiraparis reported; with the campaign approaching, groups are trying to push their causes onto the agenda.

stories.everyday: A reminder that weather services increasingly warn about impacts (flooded roads, power cuts), not just rainfall totals.
stories.rankWhy: Severe storm warnings cover several South African provinces, including the Gauteng economic hub, with risks of floods and power cuts.
stories.title: South Africa issues an orange level 5 warning for severe thunderstorms and flooding in parts of three provinces
stories.what: The South African Weather Service issued an orange level 5 impact-based warning for severe thunderstorms on Saturday, covering the far eastern Free State, western KwaZulu-Natal and the Mpumalanga Highveld, with risks of flooded roads and settlements and disruption to power and communications, The Citizen reported. Lower-level yellow warnings cover Gauteng, parts of North West, Limpopo and Mpumalanga, while extremely high fire danger is expected in the Northern Cape and parts of the Western Cape.
stories.why: Impact-based warnings rate both how likely a hazard is and how much damage it could do; level 5 on the orange tier signals significant expected impacts.

stories.everyday: As a NATO member, Türkiye's new commitments in the Middle East could affect how the alliance works, which matters to Poland's security.
stories.rankWhy: A joint defence pact linking Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, a nuclear power, reshapes security ties in a region at war.
stories.title: Türkiye's law ratifying a joint defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan takes effect; it also signs a defence pact with Qatar
stories.what: The law ratifying the 'Mecca Agreement for Joint Defense' with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia took effect on its publication in Türkiye's Official Gazette, after parliament approved it 279–119 on 5 November, Anadolu reported. Separately, Türkiye and Qatar signed five agreements in Istanbul, including a mutual defence pact signed by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.
stories.why: A mutual defence pact commits each member to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. The pacts come as Gulf states face Iranian and Houthi attacks during the Iran war, Anadolu's coverage noted; Pakistan, one of the parties to the Mecca agreement, possesses nuclear weapons.

stories.everyday: Little direct effect in Europe, but such cases test cooperation between Lebanon, Syria and Iraq.
stories.rankWhy: The killing of a prominent Iraqi critic of Iranian influence in Beirut touches sensitive regional rivalries.
stories.title: Lebanon asks Syria to hand over two suspects in the killing of former Iraqi MP Ahmed al-Alwani in Beirut
stories.what: Lebanese authorities asked Syria to extradite two Syrian nationals suspected of killing former Iraqi lawmaker Ahmed al-Alwani, whose body was found on Tuesday in a Beirut apartment, Al Jazeera reported on Friday. A judicial source said preliminary findings indicate he was strangled; a Lebanese national has been arrested, and early inquiries reportedly point to a financial motive. Al-Alwani, a Sunni politician from Ramadi and a critic of Iranian influence in Iraq, had been released in 2025 after more than a decade in prison.
stories.why: Investigators have not established who was behind the killing; Iraq's president called for a swift investigation.

stories.everyday: Drivers should allow extra time on Sunday morning; it is also a reminder to switch to winter tyres.
stories.rankWhy: A cold night with freezing fog and slippery roads affects drivers across Poland.
stories.title: IMGW forecasts sleet in places and the first widespread night frost, with freezing fog and slippery roads
stories.what: Poland's weather service IMGW forecast a cloudy Saturday with brief rain and, locally, sleet and snow pellets, with highs of 5–7°C (6°C in Warsaw), Dziennik.pl reported. Overnight into Sunday, temperatures were forecast to fall to about 0°C in most of the country and locally to −1 or −2°C, with dense freezing fog and hoarfrost making roads slippery.
stories.why: A low-pressure system over the central Baltic is bringing colder air, and clearing skies at night let heat escape, IMGW said.

stories.everyday: Shows how police use of force is checked by prosecutors.
stories.rankWhy: A legal check on police use of firearms matters mostly to those involved.
stories.title: Complaint filed over police use of a weapon to stop the Kraków attacker; prosecutors see no misconduct
stories.what: A complaint was filed with prosecutors asking them to examine whether police lawfully used a weapon against the attacker in the recent Kraków attack, TVN24 reported. Prosecutor Eryk Stasielak said it would be processed but no investigation was opened because prosecutors found no police misconduct, and Małopolska Voivode Krzysztof Klęczar praised the officers.
stories.why: In Poland, any use of firearms by police can be reviewed by prosecutors, and citizens may file complaints that must be formally examined.

stories.everyday: Polish sports bodies face similar choices if Russian teams return to competitions.
stories.rankWhy: A sports-policy decision with symbolic weight but little wider effect.
stories.title: Czech government will not ban national teams from playing Russia; hockey federation says it will refuse anyway
stories.what: Czech Sports Minister Boris Šťastný said the government will not legislate to stop Czech national teams from playing Russia, citing the autonomy of sports federations, Anadolu reported. The Czech Ice Hockey Federation had said its teams would not face Russia after a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling allowed Russian teams back into international championships; several other European hockey associations made similar decisions.
stories.why: Governments generally leave decisions on fixtures to independent sports bodies, which are bound by international federation rules.

stories.everyday: Of interest to Catholics worldwide, including in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: A papal visit draws large crowds but has limited measurable effect beyond Peru.
stories.title: Pope Leo XIV returns to Chiclayo, where he once served, during his visit to Peru
stories.what: Pope Leo XIV returned to the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo during a visit to Peru that runs until 16 November, The Rio Times reported, after leading a youth prayer vigil at Lima's National Stadium, Euronews reported.
stories.why: The Rio Times described the Chiclayo stop as a return, underlining the pope's personal ties to the city.

stories.everyday: Football fans in Poland follow the Premier League closely.
stories.rankWhy: A high-profile football appointment with little impact beyond sport.
stories.title: Manchester United appoint Mauricio Pochettino as head coach, leaving the US national team job
stories.what: Manchester United appointed Mauricio Pochettino as head coach on 13 November, a day after Michael Carrick's departure, on a two-and-a-half-year contract, Naija News reported, adding that the club reportedly paid a £7.5 million release clause. Pochettino left his role with the United States national team.
stories.why: Clubs that change coaches mid-season hope to turn results around quickly.
